chunks.title: 7. Handling the edges
chunks.text:
## 7. Handling the edges

| Symptom                                          | Cause                                              | Fix                                                                          |
| ------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| A client lib fails to bundle on `node:*`/`fs`    | Node-only code path in a browser lib               | Usually auto-stubbed; if it's a browser-usable builtin, add a polyfill (§5)  |
| A class component throws "classComponents: true" | class runtime gated off (`classComponents: false`) | remove `classComponents: false` (or set it `true`)                           |
| Native addon won't load (`better-sqlite3`)       | native `.node` binary                              | use the `node:sqlite` shim; other native deps need a Deno-native replacement |
| `pages/` routes 404                              | Pages Router plugin not enabled                    | add `@denext/pages-router` (or run `denext migrate`), or port to `app/`      |
| Duplicate-React / "no dispatcher installed"      | a React lib not routed through next-compat         | ensure the page is built via `buildNextCompatPages`                          |

---

chunks.title: 8. Known limitations
chunks.text:
## 8. Known limitations

> This is the migration-focused summary. For the full catalogue of behavioral
> divergences, the experimental/unstable API list, and the honest React DevTools
> scope, see [Known limitations](/docs/limitations).

- **App Router is the core** — the legacy Pages Router is the first-party
  `@denext/pages-router` plugin, which `denext migrate` wires up automatically
  when it finds a `pages/` tree. See [Known limitations](/docs/limitations).
- **A strict default CSP blocks external scripts/styles/images** until you opt
  the host in per route with
  `export const csp = { scriptSrc: ["https://…"], styleSrc: ["https://…"], imgSrc: ["https://…"] }`
  (`csp: "off"` in `denext.config.ts`, or a route's `export const csp = "off"`,
  disables it). See [Known differences](/docs/differences).
- **`fetch()` is uncached by default** — opt in per call with
  `next: { revalidate, tags }` or `cache: "force-cache"` (Next 15+ parity). See
  [Known differences](/docs/differences).
- **Opinionated default response headers** (`nosniff`,
  `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN`, `Referrer-Policy`, HSTS over HTTPS) are added
  unless you set your own. See [Known differences](/docs/differences).
- **Legacy provider context** (`childContextTypes`/`getChildContext`) is not
  supported; `contextType` is. See [Known limitations](/docs/limitations).
- **Type-checking a compat app isn't clean.** `deno check` still reports
  cross-library `@types/react` conflicts, because npm libraries ship their own
  React types — runtime rendering is unaffected (`skipLibCheck` is set by
  `denext migrate`).

---

chunks.title: 9. Suggested migration order
chunks.text:
## 9. Suggested migration order

1. **Probe dependencies** (§1) — know your blockers before touching code.
2. **Run `denext migrate`** in the project — it writes the `deno.json` import map
   (§3) and `denext.config.ts`, and translates `next.config.*`; it only creates
   config files and never rewrites your source unless you add `--codemod`.
3. **Port a bounded slice first** — a few public/marketing pages through the
   next-compat build; confirm dev + a production build serve and hydrate.
4. **Migrate route handlers + middleware** (§4), smoke-testing server SDKs (§6).
5. **Expand route by route**, enabling `classComponents` if a dependency needs
   it (§5).
6. **Swap native deps** (`better-sqlite3` → `node:sqlite`, §6).
7. **Test dev and a production build** at each stage.

Deploying the result: `deno task build` then `deno task start`, or a fully
static export — any host that runs Deno works. See [Deployment](/docs/deploy).

Starting fresh instead? You don't need the alias — import from `denext` and
`denext/server` directly. See [Getting started](/docs/getting-started).

> [!WARNING]
> Where denext differs from Next is documented honestly. Before a large
> migration, skim [Known differences](/docs/differences) (the deliberate
> behavioral differences) and [Known limitations](/docs/limitations) (the
> surface gaps).

Contributions and issues welcome — see the
[main README](https://github.com/Brainwires/denext).

This guide covers moving an existing **Remix (v2, or React Router v7 framework
mode)** application to [denext](https://github.com/Brainwires/denext), a
from-scratch Next.js-style framework for Deno with zero runtime npm
dependencies. It reflects what `denext migrate --from remix` actually does
today, including its honest limits.

The short version: **your data model stays as it is.** Loaders and actions keep
running on the server, `useLoaderData`, `<Form>`, `useFetcher`, sessions, and
`defer` keep working, because denext ships a first-party `denext/remix` runtime
that implements Remix's surface on denext primitives. What moves is the
**route tree**: `app/routes/*` is relocated to denext's folder-per-segment
conventions and each route module is split into a server half and a client
half. That transform is automated and reported, so the work is in reviewing
the report and validating the edges.

---

chunks.title: 1. Before you start: is your app a good fit?
chunks.text:
## 1. Before you start: is your app a good fit?

`denext migrate` recognizes a Remix app from any of these signals, in order:

- a `@remix-run/*` dependency in `package.json`;
- a `remix.config.js` / `.mjs` / `.ts`;
- a React Router v7 framework install (`react-router` or `@react-router/*` plus a
  `react-router.config.ts` / `.js`);
- the structural signature `app/root.tsx` + `app/routes/`.

Remix is checked **before** the Vite-SPA detector, because a Remix-Vite app also
carries a `vite.config`, which would otherwise be taken for a client-only SPA.
Pass `--from remix` when you want to force the path regardless.

Two install-shape requirements apply to every migrate path, not only Remix:

- **Apps with an installed `node_modules`** (most real apps) need
  `--node-modules-dir=none` on the `deno run` that launches the CLI, so Deno
  does not enter manual-`node_modules` mode and lose the CLI's own build
  dependencies. Your app's `node_modules` is untouched either way.
- **Yarn Plug'n'Play is unsupported.** denext resolves the app's dependencies
  from `node_modules` on disk, and PnP does not create one. Migrate aborts with
  a message naming the fix: add `nodeLinker: node-modules` to `.yarnrc.yml` and
  reinstall.

Anything in your app that is not Remix-specific (npm React UI libraries, server
SDKs, databases) follows the same rules as a Next.js migration. Read
the Next.js migration guide's
[§1 (the dependency probes)](/docs/migrating#1-before-you-start-is-your-app-a-good-fit),
[§5 (real npm React libraries through the compat build)](/docs/migrating#5-running-real-npm-react-libraries-next-compat-build),
and [§6 (server-side dependencies on Deno)](/docs/migrating#6-server-side-dependencies-on-deno) for that side; this guide does not repeat
them.

---

chunks.title: 2. Compatibility at a glance
chunks.text:
## 2. Compatibility at a glance

| Remix surface                                                                                  | Status                                                |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| Flat routes, dot-nested routes, v2 folder routes (`route.tsx`)                                 | ✅ relocated to `app/**/page.tsx` + `layout.tsx`      |
| `$param`, `$` splat, `_index`, pathless `_layout`, `[.]` escapes                               | ✅                                                    |
| Trailing-`_` layout break-out (`dashboard_.settings`)                                          | ⚠️ flattened and flagged for review                   |
| `loader` / `action` (server-side, `json`, `redirect`, `data`, thrown `Response`)               | ✅ run on the server, unchanged                       |
| `useLoaderData`, `useActionData`, `useRouteLoaderData`, `useMatches`                           | ✅ (Remix-canonical route ids preserved)              |
| `<Form>`, `useSubmit`, `useNavigation`, `useFetcher` / `useFetchers`, `useRevalidator`         | ✅ backed by denext Server Actions                    |
| `<Link>`, `<NavLink>`, `useNavigate`, `useLocation`, `useParams`, `useSearchParams`, `useHref` | ✅                                                    |
| `<Outlet>`, `useOutletContext`, nested layouts                                                 | ✅                                                    |
| `ErrorBoundary`, `useRouteError`, `isRouteErrorResponse`                                       | ✅ mapped to `error.tsx`                              |
| v1 `CatchBoundary` / `useCatch`                                                                | ✅ renders, flagged: fold into `ErrorBoundary`        |
| `defer` + `<Await>`, `useAsyncValue`, `useAsyncError`                                          | ✅ streams; payload finalizes whole (see §8)          |
| `shouldRevalidate`                                                                             | ✅ honored; always-revalidate is the default          |
| `useBlocker`                                                                                   | ✅ in-app navigation + back/forward; not hard unload  |
| `meta` / `links` / `headers` / `handle`                                                        | ✅ `meta` bridged to `generateMetadata`; root flagged |
| Cookies and sessions (`createCookie`, `createCookieSessionStorage`, memory/custom storage)     | ✅ from `denext/remix/server`                         |
| `unstable_parseMultipartFormData` + memory upload handler                                      | ✅                                                    |
| Resource routes (loader/action, no component)                                                  | ✅ become an API `route.ts`                           |
| `<Meta>`, `<Links>`, `<Scripts>`, `<ScrollRestoration>`, `<LiveReload>`                        | ✅ stripped; denext owns the document                 |
| `@remix-run/css-bundle` (`cssBundleHref`)                                                      | ✅ resolves to `undefined`; denext handles CSS        |
| `entry.server.*` / `entry.client.*`                                                            | deleted; denext supplies both entries                 |
| Prisma                                                                                         | ✅ auto-rewired to the Deno client (see §8)           |

---

chunks.title: 3. The command, and what it writes
chunks.text:
## 3. The command, and what it writes

```sh
# in the Remix project root
deno run --node-modules-dir=none -A jsr:@denext/denext@^2/cli migrate --from remix
deno task dev
```

Commit before you run it. The Remix path rewrites `app/` in place, and a clean
working tree makes the transform a single reviewable diff.

Config, written the same way as the Next path:

- **`deno.json`**, unless a hand-authored one already exists (a previously
  migrate-generated one is overwritten, so re-running is idempotent). It
  carries `dev` / `build` / `export` / `start` tasks, `nodeModulesDir: "auto"`,
  `react-jsx` compiler options with `skipLibCheck`, and the import map: the
  `denext` / `denext/server` / `denext/client` entries, **`denext/remix` and
  `denext/remix/server`** (the runtime the generated files import), the
  `react` / `react-dom` / `next/*` family aliases, your `tsconfig` path
  aliases, and a pinned `npm:name@version` passthrough for the app's own
  dependencies. `@remix-run/*` and `@react-router/*` are **dropped** from those
  pins: their route and data model is ported, not run.
- **`denext.config.ts`** with `compatibilityMode: true` (never clobbering an
  existing one).
- **`.gitignore`** entries for `.denext/` and `out/`, and a `.vscode` Deno LSP
  setting, appended only when missing.

Then the part that is unique to Remix: the route-tree transform (§4). When it
finishes, the CLI prints a report:

```
▸ Remix detected — route tree transformed to run on the denext/remix runtime.
  routes converted: 9 · app/root.tsx → app/layout.tsx · loaders: 3, actions: 1 (preserved & wired)
  each route → a server wrapper + a client component + a server data module (loader/action run on denext).
  removed: app/entry.server.tsx, app/entry.client.tsx
  ⚠️  review notes (2):
    · (auth)/login: pathless "_auth" → route group "(auth)"
    · dashboard/settings: layout break-out "dashboard_" (trailing _) flattened to "dashboard" — review nesting
```

Read the review notes before starting the app; §7 explains each kind.

---

chunks.title: 4. How the route tree is transformed
chunks.text: ## 4. How the route tree is transformed

chunks.title: 4.1 Naming conventions
chunks.text:
### 4.1 Naming conventions

Every module under `app/routes/` is a route: flat files (`about.tsx`,
`concerts.$city.tsx`), and the v2 folder form (`concerts.$city/route.tsx`, with
the folder's other files left as co-located modules). Files ending in `.css`,
`.server.*`, or `.client.*` are skipped as non-routes. Each route stem is parsed
into denext folder segments:

| Remix stem            | denext folder             | Note                                              |
| --------------------- | ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| `_index`              | `app/page.tsx`            | index of its parent segment                       |
| `about`               | `app/about/page.tsx`      |                                                   |
| `concerts.$city`      | `app/concerts/[city]/`    | dot nesting becomes folders; `$param` → `[param]` |
| `concerts._index`     | `app/concerts/page.tsx`   |                                                   |
| `concerts`            | `app/concerts/layout.tsx` | a route others nest under becomes the layout      |
| `files.$`             | `app/files/[...splat]/`   | a bare `$` is the catch-all                       |
| `_auth.login`         | `app/(auth)/login/`       | pathless layout → route group (no URL segment)    |
| `dashboard_.settings` | `app/dashboard/settings/` | trailing `_` break-out flattened and **flagged**  |
| `sitemap[.]xml`       | `app/sitemap.xml/`        | `[.]` escapes are unescaped                       |

A non-index route becomes a **layout** exactly when another route's path starts
with its own; otherwise it is a page. The layout keeps its `<Outlet />`, which
the runtime maps to the nested subtree.

chunks.title: 4.2 The three-file split
4.3 `route.ts` beside a page with an `action`
chunks.text:
### 4.3 `route.ts` beside a page with an `action`

In Remix a POST to a route's URL runs its action. denext serves a page's GET
from `page.tsx`, so a page route that exports an `action` also gets a generated
`route.ts` with a single `POST` handler
(`runActionResponse(data.action, request, ctx.params)`), the URL params
threaded from the matched pattern. That is what keeps a **cross-route**
`fetcher.submit` or `<Form action="/other">`, and the no-JavaScript form post
to another page, working. A redirecting cross-route action is followed as a
soft navigation. Layout routes do not get one.

chunks.title: 4.4 Resource routes
chunks.text:
### 4.4 Resource routes

A route module with a `loader` or `action` but no default component is a
resource route. It becomes a denext API route: `page.data.ts` (or
`layout.data.ts`) plus a `route.ts` exporting `GET` (`runLoaderResponse`) and
/ or `POST` (`runActionResponse`), and the report notes the conversion.

chunks.title: 4.5 `ErrorBoundary` → `error.tsx`
chunks.text:
### 4.5 `ErrorBoundary` → `error.tsx`

A route exporting `ErrorBoundary` (or a v1 `CatchBoundary`) gets an
`error.tsx` that renders the boundary through `RemixErrorProvider`, so
`useRouteError`, `isRouteErrorResponse`, and `useCatch` read the caught value.
When a route has both, only `ErrorBoundary` is wired (§7).

chunks.title: 4.6 `app/root.tsx` → `app/layout.tsx`
chunks.text:
### 4.6 `app/root.tsx` → `app/layout.tsx`

`<Meta />`, `<Links />`, `<Scripts />`, `<ScrollRestoration />`, and
`<LiveReload />` are stripped: denext owns the document and injects its own
head and scripts. A `meta` export is bridged to `generateMetadata`. Then one of
two shapes is emitted:

- A **pure document shell** (no hooks, no JSX event handlers, no loader or
  action) becomes a plain **server** layout: the `<html>` / `<head>` / `<body>`
  wrapper is reduced to its body children (denext supplies the document
  element), `<Outlet />` becomes `{children}`, and the component signature
  gains `{ children }`.
- A root that **needs the client** (a hook, an `onClick`, a loader for the
  current user) goes through the same split as a route:
  `layout.client.tsx` + `layout.data.ts` + a `layout.tsx` wrapper calling
  `RemixLayout` with id `root`. Its `<Outlet />` keeps working through
  `OutletProvider`.

A root that exports **`Layout`** keeps it: the migrated layout renders `Layout`
around both the app and the `ErrorBoundary`, as Remix does. The `<html>`,
`<head>`, and `<body>` attributes it writes reach the **real** document element
and keep updating after hydration, so a theme class toggled on `<html>` behaves
as it did. A root `links()` export becomes head tags, and a `meta()` export
receives its `matches` argument.

`entry.server.*` and `entry.client.*` are deleted; denext provides both
entries. Their startup statements are not lost: what `entry.server.tsx` ran
at module load (an `init()`, a `global.ENV` assignment) becomes a denext
`instrumentation.ts`, and what `entry.client.tsx` ran (a Sentry init) becomes
`instrumentation-client.ts`. After the routes are written, every remaining `.ts` / `.tsx` / `.js` /
`.jsx` file under `app/` (sessions, utils, shared components) has its
`@remix-run/*` and `react-router` imports remapped too, and the report counts
how many files that touched.

chunks.title: 4.7 remix-flat-routes and colocation
chunks.text:
### 4.7 remix-flat-routes and colocation

The `remix-flat-routes` convention converts too: a `users+/` folder becomes the
`users` segment, its `_layout.tsx` and `index.tsx` become that segment's
`layout.tsx` and `page.tsx`, a layout break-out folder (`$username_+`) is
handled like the flat trailing-`_` form and flagged the same way, and
`__ignored` files are left out of the route tree.

Colocation survives. A route folder's non-route modules — a `login.server.ts`,
a component, an image — are moved to `app/_routes/`, which is not a route
segment, and every import of them is re-based to the new depth. Where one route
module imported another for a constant, a component, or a type, that import is
repointed at the module that now holds it after the three-file split, so the
reference keeps resolving.

---

chunks.title: 5. The import map
chunks.text:
## 5. The import map

Specifiers are remapped mechanically, in route modules and across the rest of
`app/`. Only the module path changes; the named exports keep their Remix
names.

| Remix specifier                                                                            | denext module         | Notes                                                                                                                |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `@remix-run/react`                                                                         | `denext/remix`        | hooks, `Link`, `NavLink`, `Form`, `Outlet`, `Await`, the document components (rendered as nothing)                   |
| `@remix-run/node`, `@remix-run/cloudflare`, `@remix-run/deno`, `@remix-run/server-runtime` | `denext/remix/server` | `json`, `redirect`, `replace`, `redirectDocument`, `data`, `defer`, cookies, session storage, multipart form parsing |
| `@remix-run/css-bundle`                                                                    | `denext/remix/server` | `cssBundleHref` is `undefined`; denext builds CSS itself                                                             |
| `react-router`, `react-router-dom`                                                         | `denext/remix`        | covers React Router v7 framework-mode apps                                                                           |

`deno.json` also aliases `react`, `react-dom`, and `react-is` to denext, exactly
as in the Next.js guide's [§3](/docs/migrating#3-project-setup), so your own
`import { useState } from "react"` and your npm React libraries resolve to the
single denext React.

---

chunks.title: 6. What carries over
chunks.text:
## 6. What carries over

- **Loaders and actions** run on the server with the request, the params, and
  the Remix helpers they already use. `json`, `redirect`, `replace`, `data`,
  and a thrown `Response` behave as in Remix; response cookies set by a thrown
  redirect are forwarded.
- **`<Form>` and `useSubmit`** are backed by denext Server Actions. A mutating
  `<Form>` with no explicit `action` binds to the current route's action;
  submitting sets `useNavigation()` to `submitting`, stores the result for
  `useActionData`, and triggers a revalidation that carries the form method and
  action into `shouldRevalidate`. `method="get"` is a soft search navigation.
  The DOM `action` attribute is the Server Action's endpoint URL, so the form
  still posts without JavaScript. `reloadDocument` opts out.
- **Data and navigation hooks**: `useLoaderData`, `useActionData`,
  `useRouteLoaderData`, `useMatches`, `useParams`, `useLocation`,
  `useNavigate`, `useSearchParams`, `useHref`, `useResolvedPath`,
  `useFormAction`, `useNavigation`, `useRevalidator`, `useFetcher` (same-route
  action, cross-route `load` and `submit`, following a redirecting action),
  `useFetchers`, and `useBlocker`.
- **Sessions and cookies**: `createCookie`, `isCookie`,
  `createCookieSessionStorage`, `createMemorySessionStorage`,
  `createSessionStorage`, `createSession`, `isSession`, and
  `unstable_parseMultipartFormData` with the memory upload handler, from
  `denext/remix/server`.
- **`defer` and `<Await>`**: a `defer()` promise leaves a placeholder so the
  shell flushes immediately with the `<Await>` fallback; the content streams in
  as its Suspense boundary resolves, and the resolved value is written into the
  tail Flight payload so hydration sees real data. A rejection drives
  `errorElement` through `useAsyncError`.
- **Nested routes and layouts**: `<Outlet />` in a layout renders the nested
  subtree, `<Outlet context>` / `useOutletContext` work, and an ancestor's
  loader data is readable from a nested route through `useMatches` and
  `useRouteLoaderData`, including during the Flight serialization pass.
- **`ErrorBoundary`** maps to `error.tsx` with `useRouteError` and
  `isRouteErrorResponse`; **`meta`** to `generateMetadata`.
- **`remix-flat-routes` and colocation**: the `users+/` folder convention,
  `_layout.tsx` / `index.tsx`, layout break-outs (`$username_+`), and
  `__ignored` files convert, and colocated modules move to `app/_routes/` with
  every import re-based (§4.7).
- **Route-relative links**: `<Link to="new">`, `useNavigate`, and
  `useResolvedPath` resolve against the route's own pathname, and `..` climbs a
  route, exactly as in Remix.
- **The custom server's load context**: a `getLoadContext` becomes a root
  `load-context.ts` (`defineLoadContext`), so loaders keep reading their
  `context`. `context.serverBuild` is denext's synthesized Remix `ServerBuild`
  (`remixServerBuild()`), which is what `@nasa-gcn/remix-seo` reads to generate
  a sitemap. A value the old server read off the Express request has no
  equivalent and is left as a `TODO` stub to fill in.
- **Assets and Tailwind**: `import logo from "./logo.svg"` and a
  `styles.css?url` import are served under `/_denext/client/assets/`, and a
  Tailwind v3 stylesheet is compiled through the project's own `tailwindcss`.
  A Prisma app gets the Rust-free Deno client and has its SQL migrations
  applied by `deno task prisma:setup` (§8).

---

chunks.title: 7. The review warnings
chunks.text:
## 7. The review warnings

The transform is assisted, not silent. Everything it cannot map one-to-one is
reported, never guessed at. The notes you can see, and what to do about each:

| Note                                                     | Meaning                                                                                               | What to do                                                                                 |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `pathless "_auth" → route group "(auth)"`                | A pathless layout became a route group; the URL is unchanged.                                         | Informational. Confirm the group's `layout.tsx` is what you expect.                        |
| `layout break-out "dashboard_" (trailing _) flattened`   | denext has no direct equivalent of opting a segment out of its parent layout; the name was flattened. | Check the nesting: the route now renders inside the parent layout.                         |
| `v1 CatchBoundary → error.tsx (via useCatch)`            | The route only has a v1 `CatchBoundary`; it is wired and still renders.                               | Migrate it to a v2 `ErrorBoundary` with `isRouteErrorResponse` when convenient.            |
| `v1 CatchBoundary alongside ErrorBoundary`               | Both exist; only `ErrorBoundary` is wired to `error.tsx`.                                             | Fold the `CatchBoundary` cases into `ErrorBoundary` using `isRouteErrorResponse`.          |
| `layout renders no <Outlet/> — nested routes won't show` | A route became a layout (others nest under it) but its component has no `<Outlet />`.                 | Add `<Outlet />`, or restructure so the route is not a layout.                             |
| `resource route (no component) → generated a route.ts`   | A loader/action-only module became an API route.                                                      | Informational. Verify its method(s) and the response shape.                                |
| `root: meta/links exports — ported via generateMetadata` | The root's `meta` is bridged; `links` has no direct denext equivalent in `generateMetadata`.          | Look at the rendered `<head>`; move stylesheet or preload links into the layout if needed. |
| `rewrote @remix-run/* imports in N shared module(s)`     | Non-route files under `app/` were rewritten to the runtime specifiers.                                | Informational. Diff them once.                                                             |

The CLI prints up to twelve notes and a count of the rest.

---

chunks.title: 8. Known limitations
chunks.text:
## 8. Known limitations

> This is the migration-focused summary. The full statement lives in
> [Known limitations → "Remix and React Router"](/docs/limitations#remix-and-react-router).

- **`shouldRevalidate` is honored, and always-revalidate is the default.** On a
  client revalidation (a soft navigation or `useRevalidator`), the client echoes
  each route's prior loader data and params with the request (in headers, or a
  POST body when the echo is too large for headers). When a route's
  `shouldRevalidate` returns `false` the server skips that loader's work and
  renders from the echoed data. First paint, hard navigations, routes without
  `shouldRevalidate`, and an explicit `true` always run the loader, so nothing
  is ever stale.
- **Deferred data is whole at the end.** The `<Await>` content streams
  progressively and first paint is not blocked, but the Flight payload
  (`#__denext_flight`) is emitted once all boundaries resolve. A soft
  navigation to a deferred route therefore carries the resolved value rather
  than re-streaming the chunk.
- **`useBlocker` guards in-app navigations and browser back/forward, not a
  hard unload.** A registered blocker vetoes `<Link>`, `useNavigate`, and
  `<Form>` navigations and undoes a popstate until `proceed()`; one active
  blocker, matching react-router. A reload or tab close is still the browser's
  own `beforeunload` prompt; add one where you need it.
- **`links` has no automatic port.** A route's `links` export is moved into
  the data module and kept, but only `meta` is bridged into
  `generateMetadata`; stylesheet and preload links need a home in the layout.
- **`headers` and `handle` are carried, not interpreted as Remix does.**
  `handle` is threaded to `useMatches`; a `headers` export is preserved in the
  data module for you to apply through denext's `headers()` or middleware.
- **Prisma is auto-migrated to the Rust-free Deno client.** The schema
  generator becomes the ESM `prisma-client` with `queryCompiler` and
  `driverAdapters`, every `@prisma/client` import is repointed, the adapter is
  injected at each `new PrismaClient()`, and `deno.json` gets the `links` shim,
  npm pins, and a `prisma:setup` task. Run `deno task prisma:setup` once. Only
  runtime source under `app/` / `src/` / `lib/` is rewritten (a `prisma/seed.ts`
  is left for Node), a `new PrismaClient(<non-object>)` is flagged for a
  one-line manual adapter add, and non-SQLite datasources need their own driver
  adapter.
- **Everything that is not Remix-specific** (the default Content-Security-Policy
  and response headers, uncached `fetch()` by default, class components in npm
  libraries, native addons) is exactly as documented in
  the Next.js migration guide's
  [§5](/docs/migrating#5-running-real-npm-react-libraries-next-compat-build),
  [§7](/docs/migrating#7-handling-the-edges), and
  [§8](/docs/migrating#8-known-limitations).

---

chunks.title: 9. How this differs from the Next path
chunks.text:
## 9. How this differs from the Next path

| Aspect             | Next.js path                                                                                                          | Remix path                                                                                           |
| ------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| What migrate does  | **Config only by default.** Writes `deno.json` + `denext.config.ts`; source is untouched unless you pass `--codemod`. | **Config + a route-tree transform.** Rewrites `app/` in place; routes are relocated and split.       |
| File conventions   | Already denext's own (App Router).                                                                                    | `app/routes/*` + `root.tsx` are converted to `app/**/page.tsx` + `layout.tsx`.                       |
| Data model         | Server Components and Server Actions, as written.                                                                     | Loaders and actions, preserved and run by the `denext/remix` runtime.                                |
| Framework imports  | `next/*` aliased in the import map; optional `--codemod` rewrites them to `denext`.                                   | `@remix-run/*` and `react-router` rewritten in the source to `denext/remix` / `denext/remix/server`. |
| Old toolchain deps | Inert toolchain, lint, and `@types/*` deps are dropped from the pins.                                                 | The same, plus `@remix-run/*` / `@react-router/*`.                                                   |
| Report             | Files written, deps classified.                                                                                       | Plus routes converted, loaders and actions wired, entries removed, and review notes (§7).            |
| Re-running         | Idempotent (generated files carry a sentinel).                                                                        | Config is idempotent; the route transform runs once, on a tree that still has `app/routes/`.         |

Both paths share the `deno.json` shape, the npm passthrough, the compat build
for real npm React libraries, and the Prisma wiring.

---

chunks.title: 10. Suggested migration order
chunks.text:
## 10. Suggested migration order

1. **Commit**, then check the install shape: a real `node_modules` (no Yarn
   PnP), and `--node-modules-dir=none` on the migrate command (§1).
2. **Probe non-Remix dependencies** with the probes in
   the Next.js migration guide's
   [§1](/docs/migrating#1-before-you-start-is-your-app-a-good-fit) so you know your
   blockers before touching code.
3. **Run `denext migrate --from remix`** (§3) and read the review notes (§7).
4. **Diff `app/`.** Skim one converted route of each kind (a page with a loader,
   one with an action, a layout, the root) so the three-file split is familiar.
5. **`deno task dev`**, then walk the app: navigation, a form submit, a fetcher,
   a deferred route, an error boundary.
6. **Address the notes**: break-outs, `CatchBoundary`, root `links`, layouts
   without an `<Outlet />`.
7. **Build and serve** with `deno task build` then `deno task start`, and test
   the no-JavaScript form path once.
8. Write **new** routes the denext way (a Server Component in `page.tsx`)
   alongside the migrated ones; there is no need to convert the old ones.

Contributions and issues welcome. See the main
[README](https://github.com/Brainwires/denext).

Coming from React Native or Expo? Read [Coming from React Native](/docs/coming-from-react-native) for the concept map, [denext vs React Native](/docs/vs-react-native) for who should switch (and who should not), and [React Native / Expo apps](/docs/react-native) to build an existing Expo app with `denext migrate --from expo`. The desktop target (`denext desktop`, `denext/desktop/updater`) is on [Desktop apps](/docs/desktop).

> **Platform status.** iOS is verified on a physical iPhone: live reload with `denext mobile dev`, the capabilities [`examples/mobile`](https://github.com/Brainwires/denext/tree/main/examples/mobile) exercises, push, deep links, auth sessions, the share extension, a configurable widget, a Live Activity (including one started by a push-to-start push) and a signed over-the-air update. The 2.11 surface ran on an iPhone 16e on 2026-09-27: the keyboard (a chat composer and a form), system bars following the theme, the system and in-page dialogs, pull-to-refresh, permissions and opening Settings, local notifications (actions and tap routing), geolocation, orientation lock, the privacy screen, the tracking prompt, the review sheet, saving to Photos, `VirtualList` (an exact `scrollToIndex` on 100,000 rows, flings without blank frames, a chat list, sticky headers) and the stack, tabs and sheet of [native-feel navigation](/docs/navigation-native). On 2026-09-28 [`examples/native-views`](https://github.com/Brainwires/denext/tree/main/examples/native-views) ran there: [native views](#native-views) in a `VirtualList`, the video drawn under the page with AVKit's controls, a vertical swipe on it scrolling the list (`scrollPassthrough`), and the views kept across a Fast Refresh edit. The same day an Expo SDK 57 app in [React Native mode](/docs/react-native) (`examples/expo-app`) ran there: its tabs, deep links (cold start and running), haptics, alerts and share, AsyncStorage kept across launches (on [durable storage](#durable-storage)), a focused field scrolled above the keyboard, and the top safe-area inset applied after first paint. Built and unit-tested but not yet run on the phone: native modules, native context menus, `SystemIcon`, font scaling, biometrics, native sign-in, in-app purchases, crash reporting, background tasks and background location, and the bottom safe-area inset. Android is compiled and unit-tested, not run on a device: its halves of `denext/mobile` and of the generators have not run on Android at all, and a whole-app comparison ran on an emulator only. The details, and every open limit, are in [Known limitations](/docs/limitations) (Mobile) and the open work in the [roadmap](https://github.com/Brainwires/denext/blob/main/ROADMAP.md).

chunks.title: Quickstart: from an empty directory to a phone
chunks.text:
## Quickstart: from an empty directory to a phone

You need Deno, Node.js (Capacitor's CLI is an npm package, and `denext mobile` runs it through `npx`), and the platform toolchains: Xcode for iOS, Android Studio for Android. The shell loads denext's static export (`denext export` → `out/`), so the app inside it is static files: route handlers, Server Actions and per-request rendering need a server the app calls over the network. A multi-page export routes correctly in the shell: Capacitor answers every path without an extension with the root `index.html` (it assumes a single-page app), so the native files denext writes serve `/about` from `about/index.html` (or `about.html`); an app with no denext native plugin gets them from `denext mobile add export-routes` (`denext mobile doctor` flags a shell without them).

**1. Scaffold.** `--capacitor` adds a `capacitor.config.ts` that bundles the export (`webDir: "out"`) into the native shells, a `package.json` pinning Capacitor 8 (`^8.5.2`), an `export` task and the `mobile:*` tasks. Add `--desktop` to scaffold the desktop target too. Change `appId` and `appName` in `capacitor.config.ts` before you add the platforms: the app id becomes the bundle id and the Android package name.

```bash
deno run -A jsr:@denext/denext/cli create my-app --capacitor
cd my-app
```

**2. Optional: a client-only app.** The scaffold is an App Router app, exported to static HTML. An app that renders everything in the browser can use [SPA mode](/docs/spa) instead, as [`examples/mobile`](https://github.com/Brainwires/denext/tree/main/examples/mobile) does:

```ts
// denext.config.ts
import type { DenextConfig } from "denext/server";

export default {
  mode: "spa",
  spa: {
    entry: "./src/main.tsx",
    // viewport-fit=cover lets the page draw under the notch; SAFE_AREA_CSS pads it back.
    head: `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1, viewport-fit=cover" />`,
    precompress: false, // the webview loads files from the app bundle, never the .gz siblings
    ota: true, // stamp out/_denext/ota.json for over-the-air updates
  },
} satisfies DenextConfig;
```

**3. Add the native platforms.** Install the npm packages, export once so the `webDir` exists when Capacitor copies it, then add each platform once:

```bash
deno install                # Capacitor's CLI + platforms are npm packages
deno task export            # out/
deno run -A --node-modules-dir npm:@capacitor/cli@^8.5.2 add ios       # once
deno run -A --node-modules-dir npm:@capacitor/cli@^8.5.2 add android   # once
```

**4. Run it on a phone.** Sync after every change to the web app, then run from the IDE:

```bash
deno task mobile:sync       # export, stamp the OTA manifest, copy out/ into ios/ and android/
deno task mobile:ios        # open in Xcode: pick your team under Signing, choose the phone, Run
deno task mobile:android    # open in Android Studio
```

**5. Live reload.** Point the installed app at `denext dev` instead of the bundled export, so every edit reloads on the phone (the phone and the computer on the same Wi-Fi). On iOS the first session changes `Info.plist`, so run the app from Xcode once more; [Live reload on a device](#live-reload-on-a-device) has the details.

```bash
denext mobile dev --lan     # Ctrl-C puts capacitor.config back
```

**6. Add native capabilities.** Each one installs a Capacitor plugin (or writes denext's own native plugin) and wires the native project; the matching function in `denext/mobile` then works in the shell and falls back to a browser API on the web. A plugin is native code, so build and run the app again afterwards.

```bash
denext mobile add --list
denext mobile add haptics share secure-store
```

Commit `ios/` and `android/`: Capacitor 8 builds iOS with Swift Package Manager, and the native projects are yours to edit. The scaffolded `.gitignore` ignores only their build outputs and the web assets `mobile:sync` copies in; Capacitor's own generated `.gitignore` files cover the rest. The webview loads files straight from the app bundle, so the export ships no precompressed `.gz` siblings: the App Router export never writes them, and a SPA-mode app turns them off with `spa: { precompress: false }`.

> A complete project wired for web + desktop + mobile is [`examples/native`](https://github.com/Brainwires/denext/tree/main/examples/native), and [`examples/mobile`](https://github.com/Brainwires/denext/tree/main/examples/mobile) exercises every `denext/mobile` capability on one page, with the commands that made its shell. Native builds are experimental.

chunks.title: Live reload on a device
chunks.text:
## Live reload on a device

During development the app can load straight from `denext dev` instead of the bundled export, the way a React Native app attaches to Metro: every edit reloads on the phone. `denext mobile dev` starts the dev server (or attaches to one already answering on the port), writes `server: { url, cleartext: true }` into `capacitor.config.*` and runs `npx cap copy`:

```bash
denext mobile dev --lan            # a physical device on the same Wi-Fi
denext mobile dev                  # localhost: the iOS simulator (or Android + adb reverse)
denext mobile dev web --dir mobile # the denext project in web/, Capacitor in mobile/
```

Then run the app from Xcode (or `npx cap run ios`/`android`). The page origin *is* the dev server, so the reload stream and the dev origin check work unchanged. The config edit is temporary: Ctrl-C, `SIGTERM` or an error writes the original bytes back and runs `cap copy` again, so a release build never ships the dev URL. A run killed outright leaves a backup in `.denext/`; the next `mobile dev` (or `mobile dev --restore`) restores it first. `cap copy` needs the `webDir` built once. The restore does not depend on it: it takes the dev URL out of the native config copies (`ios/App/App/capacitor.config.json`, `android/app/src/main/assets/capacitor.config.json`) itself, so they stop pointing at the dev server even when the closing `cap copy` fails; then run your export and `npx cap copy` before a release build. `denext mobile build --release` (and the fastlane lanes, which run it) refuses while that backup is on disk, or while the Capacitor config's `server` names a LAN / loopback `http` URL or sets `cleartext`, unless a flavor's `serverUrl` sets the server on purpose.

On iOS, `cleartext` does nothing (it is Android's `usesCleartextTraffic`, which `cap copy` writes for you). A WebView reaches a LAN dev server only when `ios/App/App/Info.plist` has `NSAppTransportSecurity` → `NSAllowsLocalNetworking` (App Transport Security) and a `NSLocalNetworkUsageDescription` (without one, iOS 14+ silently denies local-network requests and the app hangs on its splash screen). `mobile dev` adds both for the session, merging into an existing ATS dict and keeping an existing description, and puts the plist back with the config. A changed Info.plist is a native change: rebuild and run the app from Xcode (it prints so). Xcode opens `ios/App/App.xcworkspace` for a CocoaPods project and `ios/App/App.xcodeproj` for a Swift Package Manager one (Capacitor 8's default), and the printed steps name whichever exists.

Without the helper, `denext dev --lan` binds the machine's LAN IPv4, allows it through the dev origin gate, and prints its URL with a QR code to scan. By default the dev assets (`/_denext/*`) answer only a loopback `Host`: that is the DNS-rebinding defense, and it is why a phone pointed at `--host 0.0.0.0` used to render a dead page. An explicit `--host` now allows the host it binds (`0.0.0.0` allows this machine's own addresses), and [`allowedDevOrigins`](/docs/config#dev-server) (or `--allowed-dev-origin`) lists any other host. Anything on the network that can reach an allowed address could load the dev app and its source, so a network bind carries a session token: the printed URL and its QR code end in `?__denext_dev=…`. The first request with it sets an HttpOnly, `SameSite=Strict` cookie and redirects to the clean URL; from then on every request from another machine — pages, `/_denext/*`, the module graph, the reload stream and the Live socket — needs that cookie (or the `x-denext-dev-token` header) and is a `403` without it. Requests from this machine's loopback need nothing. The token is new on each run. `denext mobile dev --lan` writes the tokened URL into `server.url`, and `denext desktop dev --lan` sends it from the window's dev proxy.

chunks.title: The `denext/mobile` runtime
Platform-specific files
chunks.text:
## Platform-specific files

A component that differs a lot on a phone can have a file of its own: `BigButton.ios.tsx`, `BigButton.android.tsx`, or `BigButton.mobile.tsx` for both. `denext mobile build ios` exports with the `ios` target before `cap sync`, so the shell's `webDir` holds an export that resolves `./BigButton` to `.ios`, then `.mobile`, then `.web`, then the plain file, and leaves the other variants out; `denext export --platform ios` builds the same export by hand. See [platform-specific files](/docs/platform-files).

chunks.title: Native capabilities
chunks.text:
## Native capabilities

`denext/mobile` also wraps the common Capacitor plugins. Each function calls the official plugin inside the shell and falls back to a browser API (or does nothing) on the web, so the same code runs in both places. `denext mobile add` installs the plugins: it finds the project (the folder with `capacitor.config.*`, or `--dir`), refuses a `@capacitor/core` major other than 8, adds the packages with the package manager the nearest lockfile names (looking up to the repository root, so a pnpm / yarn / bun workspace's lockfile counts; else a `packageManager` field; else npm), declares any Android permissions they need, and runs `npx cap sync`. The install runs in the Capacitor project folder. Before the web export exists (no `index.html` in the config's `webDir`), sync would stop at the missing folder, so it runs `npx cap update` instead (the native half of sync) and says what is left: `denext export`, then `npx cap sync`.

```bash
denext mobile add --list                    # the capabilities and their plugins
denext mobile add haptics share network --dry-run   # print the plan, change nothing
denext mobile add haptics share network secure-store
```

> **Warning:** Running the CLI straight from JSR inside a Node workspace? Pass `--node-modules-dir=none`: without it Deno reads the workspace's `package.json`, fails to resolve denext's own `npm:` imports from its `node_modules`, and (with a `pnpm-workspace.yaml`) rewrites the root `package.json`.
>
> ```bash
> deno run -A --node-modules-dir=none jsr:@denext/denext/cli mobile add haptics --dry-run
> ```

- `haptic(kind)` (`haptics`): an impact, notification or selection tick; falls back to `navigator.vibrate`.
- `readClipboard()` / `writeClipboard(text)` (`clipboard`): falls back to `navigator.clipboard`.
- `share({ title, text, url })` (`share`): resolves `"shared"`, `"cancelled"`, or `"copied"` when there is no share sheet and the text went to the clipboard.
- `deviceInfo()` (`device`): platform, model, OS version; a best-effort user-agent read on the web. `application` installs `@capacitor/app` and `@capacitor/device` together, the pair `expo-application` reads (name, id, version, build, and the vendor / Android id).
- `networkStatus()` / `useNetworkStatus()` (`network`): connected and the connection type; `navigator.onLine` on the web.
- `useKeepAwake(active)` (`keep-awake`): keeps the screen on; the Screen Wake Lock API on the web.
- `hideSplash()` (`splash`): hides the launch splash when `launchAutoHide` is off.
- `secureStore.get / set / delete` (`secure-store`): the iOS Keychain / Android Keystore. On the web it is a plain IndexedDB database, which is **not** secret.
- `openSqlite(name)` (`sqlite`): a SQLite database with `exec` / `run` / `query`; `@capacitor-community/sqlite` on the device, and on the web the app's own `@sqlite.org/sqlite-wasm` on the Origin Private File System (install it yourself; without it `openSqlite` reports the engine is missing).
- `readFile` / `writeFile` / `deleteFile` / `listDir` / `downloadToFile(url, path)` (`filesystem`): the app's files in `"data"`, `"documents"` or `"cache"`, as text or base64; the Origin Private File System on the web (a top-level folder per directory).
- `pickImage({ source })` (`camera`, which also writes the camera, photo-library and microphone usage strings; the microphone one is for video recorded in the page) and `pickDocument({ types })` (`document-picker`): resolve `null` when the user cancels; a hidden file input on the web.
- Picked files and folders: in a Deno Desktop window and in browsers with the File System Access API, `pickDocument`, `saveFile` and `pickFolder` return an opaque `handle` (the `path` is display-only), and the file functions reach the item with `{ directory: { picked: handle } }` (see [Picked files and folders](/docs/desktop#picked-files-and-folders)). The iOS/Android pickers return a copy's `path` and no handle, and a `{ picked }` directory rejects `unavailable` in the shell: read a picked document with `readData: true`.
- `scanBarcode({ formats })` (`barcode`): the value and format of one code; `BarcodeDetector` over the camera on the web where the browser has it. The install raises Android's `minSdkVersion` to 26, which the scanner needs.
- `setQuickActions([...])` / `onQuickAction` / `useQuickAction` (`quick-actions`): home-screen shortcuts on a long press of the app icon, the one that cold-started the app included (the install wires `SceneDelegate.swift`); nothing on the web.

Audio, video and image editing need no plugin: Expo's `expo-audio` and `expo-video` map to `<audio>`, `<video>` and Web Audio in the WebView, and `expo-image-manipulator` to Canvas / `OffscreenCanvas`.

`browser` installs the plugin `openExternal` uses for its in-app browser. Three capabilities install the plugins behind [React Native mode](/docs/react-native#react-native-apis)'s system UI, each with an in-page fallback when its plugin is missing: `dialog` (`@capacitor/dialog`: `Alert.alert` and `Alert.prompt`), `toast` (`@capacitor/toast` ^8.0.1: `ToastAndroid.show` as the system toast on Android) and `action-sheet` (`@capacitor/action-sheet` ^8.1.1: `ActionSheetIOS.showActionSheetWithOptions` as a native sheet). None needs a usage string, a permission or a privacy-manifest entry. A new plugin is native code: ship a new app binary afterwards.

chunks.title: Keyboard, back, system bars and safe areas
chunks.text:
## Keyboard, back, system bars and safe areas

Four things a phone app needs that a browser tab mostly doesn't: staying clear of the on-screen keyboard, Android's back button and back gesture, the status and navigation bars, and the insets around the notch and the home indicator. Each works in the browser too, so the same component runs everywhere.

```bash
denext mobile add keyboard back system-bars
```

chunks.title: Keyboard
Android back and predictive back
System bars
chunks.text:
### System bars

`setSystemBars({ style, hidden, animation, bar })` drives Capacitor 8's `SystemBars`, which ships in `@capacitor/core`. `style` names the theme the bars sit over: `"dark"` for a dark app (light icons), `"light"` for a light one, `"auto"` for the device's appearance. (`expo-status-bar`'s `style` names the icons' color instead, the other way round.) `hidden` hides or shows them, `animation` (`"fade"` / `"none"`) is iOS only, and `bar` (`"status"` / `"navigation"`) limits the change to one bar. On the web it does nothing.

`useSystemBarsFollowTheme()` keeps the bars on the page's theme, re-applied on every change: the root element's `color-scheme` when it names one (a theme toggle that sets it, or `Appearance.setColorScheme` in react-native mode), else `prefers-color-scheme`. Pass the theme instead when the app decides it: `useSystemBarsFollowTheme(theme)`.

`denext mobile add system-bars` installs no package. It sets `UIViewControllerBasedStatusBarAppearance` in Info.plist (SystemBars needs it) and adds `EdgeToEdge.enable(this)` to the MainActivity, so the app draws edge to edge with transparent bars on every Android version, as Android 15 and 16 enforce for current target SDKs. Pad for the bars with the safe areas below.

chunks.title: Safe areas
chunks.text:
### Safe areas

`SAFE_AREA_CSS` (above) and `useSafeAreaInsets()` read the same values: the `--safe-area-inset-*` custom properties Capacitor 8 injects on Android (its default `insetsHandling: "css"`) when they are set, else `env(safe-area-inset-*)`. The injected values matter because Android WebView before 140 reports wrong `env()` insets; on iOS and the web they are unset and `env()` applies.

- For layout, use `SAFE_AREA_CSS`'s `--denext-safe-*` variables: CSS applies them without a render.
- When JavaScript needs the numbers (a sheet's resting height, a canvas, a gesture's edge zone), `useSafeAreaInsets()` returns `{ top, right, bottom, left }` in px, updated on rotation, resizes and when Capacitor updates its values (on Android the bottom inset drops to 0 while the keyboard is up).
- Outside a component (a store, an imperative animation), `readSafeAreaInsets()` returns the same numbers once (zeros during server rendering), and `watchSafeAreaInsets(cb)` calls `cb` at once with the current insets, then on rotation, resizes, visual-viewport changes and Capacitor's inset updates, at most once per frame and only when a value changed. It returns a function that stops it.

Both need `viewport-fit=cover` in the viewport meta.

chunks.title: Pull to refresh
Native views in the layout
chunks.text: ## Native views in the layout `NativeViewSlot` reserves a box in the page and keeps a native view on it: a map, a video player with the system controls, a camera preview, or any view type your app registers natively. The page scrolls, clips and covers the slot like any other box; its children are the web fallback, rendered on the web, during SSR, and in a shell without the plugin or without that view type. `denext mobile add native-views` installs the `DenextNativeViews` plugin (Swift and Java, registered like the other denext plugins) with the built-in `video` view; `denext mobile add native-map` adds `map` (MapKit on iOS, OpenStreetMap through osmdroid on Android, neither with an API key). ```tsx import { NativeViewSlot } from "denext/mobile"; name === "regionChange" && console.log(data)} onCommand={(command) => (recenter.current = command)} // command("setRegion", { … }) overlay={} style={{ height: 280, borderRadius: 12, overflow: "hidden" }} > {/* the web fallback */} ``` `overlay` is DOM drawn over the native view; touches on its elements stay in the page, and every other touch over the slot's visible part reaches the native view. `useNativeViewSlot(type, options)` is the same as a hook for a slot element you render yourself (it returns the refs, `status`, `placement` and `command`). `scrollPassthrough` (iOS and Android) decides which drags that start on an `"under"` or `"over"` view scroll the page instead: `"vertical"` (the default for `video`: a mostly vertical drag scrolls the list, with the page's own momentum and bounce, while taps and horizontal scrubs stay the player's), `"horizontal"`, or `"none"` (the default otherwise, so a map pans on any drag). The slot gets the matching CSS `touch-action`. On Android a drag that passes the touch slop along that axis is handed to the WebView from where it started, so the page scrolls with its own fling (compile-verified, not yet run on an Android device). Where the view is drawn (`placement`, default `"auto"`): - `"embed"` (iOS, the default there): the view is added to the native scroll view WebKit backs the slot's `overflow: scroll` element with, the approach of `@capacitor/google-maps`. The compositor moves, clips and transforms it with the page (scrolling, CSS transforms and animations included, with no lag), and page content drawn later (a sticky header, a modal) covers it. If WebKit does not back the element with a scroll view within 2 s, it falls back to `"over"`. - `"over"` (the default on Android): the view is drawn above the WebView, clipped to the part of the slot its scrolling ancestors and the viewport leave visible. It needs nothing from the page, but no DOM can draw over it: while page content covers any part of the slot (a sheet, a modal, a sticky header) the view hides. - `"under"` : the view is drawn behind the WebView, which is made transparent, and seen through the slot. DOM over the slot draws above it. The slot and every ancestor must be transparent where the slot is (a dev warning names the first one that is not); a touch over the visible part is handed to the view unless page content covers the slot. For `"under"` and `"over"` the page sends each slot's box in the content coordinates of the container it scrolls with (its nearest scrolling ancestor, or the document), which scrolling does not change. On iOS the plugin finds that container's native scroll view and follows its offset itself, in the same frame as the scroll, so fling and momentum keep the view on its slot with no message from the page. On Android the WebView's own scroll is followed the same way, but a scrolling element inside the page has no native scroll view there: the page sends its measurement each frame it scrolls, and the view trails its slot by a frame or two (see [Known limitations](/docs/limitations)). Layout changes (a resize, the keyboard, content inserted above, a CSS transition) are measured each animation frame while they happen and every 250 ms otherwise. A slot unmounted by a virtualized list destroys its view, and a new one is made when it scrolls back. The built-in views. `video`: props `src` (an absolute URL), `autoplay`, `loop`, `muted`, `controls` (default true), `fit` (`"contain"` or `"cover"`, iOS); events `ready`, `play`, `pause`, `ended`, `error`; commands `play`, `pause`, `seek`, `status`. On iOS it is an `AVPlayerViewController` with the system controls, contained in the app's view controller, and `"auto"` draws it `"under"` the WebView (a plain UIKit hierarchy that follows the page's scrolling in the same frame), so page content drawn over the slot covers it and its full-screen button and exit are AVKit's own; controls inside WebKit's scroll view (`"embed"`) do not complete a tap. The slot and its ancestors must be transparent there (a dev warning names an opaque one). On Android it is a `VideoView` with the system `MediaController`. `map`: props `latitude`, `longitude`, `zoom` (0 to 20), `markers`, `mapType` (iOS), `interactive`; events `regionChange`, `markerPress`; command `setRegion`. The map moves only when `latitude`, `longitude` or `zoom` change, so a pan is not undone by other props. OpenStreetMap's tile servers are for light use: point a production Android app at its own tile source.

chunks.title: Your own native view
Context menus
System icons
chunks.text:
## System icons

`<SystemIcon name="square.and.arrow.up" android="share" />` draws the platform's own icon. In the iOS shell with `denext mobile add system-icons` it is the real SF Symbol: the `DenextSystemIcon` plugin renders it with `UIImage(systemName:)` at the requested weight and scale and the device's pixel density, and the page uses it as a mask filled with the CSS `color` (so it follows the text color, dark mode and hover). Every render is cached natively and in the page. Everywhere else (Android, the web, a desktop window, SSR) it is a Material Symbol drawn as inline SVG.

```tsx
"use client";
import { SystemIcon } from "denext/mobile";

<SystemIcon name="house.fill" size={26} />                 // Material: home-fill (mapped)
<SystemIcon name="bell" weight="semibold" label="Alerts" /> // role="img" with a name
<SystemIcon name="cloud.sun.fill" mode="multicolor" android="partly_cloudy_day" />
```

- `size` (CSS px, default 24), `weight` (`ultralight` … `black`), `scale`, `color`, and `mode`: `monochrome` (the default mask), `hierarchical`, `palette` (`colors`) or `multicolor`.
- Without `android`, the Material Symbol is mapped from the SF Symbol name for the common icons (`house` → `home`, `square.and.arrow.up` → `share`, a `.fill` suffix to the `-fill` variant). denext ships about 75 common Material Symbols (Apache 2.0); `registerSystemIcons({ name: pathData })` adds any other from `@material-symbols/svg-400`.
- The server renders the Material Symbol, so the markup always hydrates; in the iOS shell the SF Symbol replaces it before paint once cached, and the box is hidden for the one bridge round trip of a first render. `preloadSystemIcons([...])` at startup warms the icons of the first screen.
- **Why no SF Symbols SVGs:** Apple licenses SF Symbols for use in apps on Apple platforms only, so denext ships none of their artwork; iOS draws them itself, and every other platform gets Material Symbols.

Sending push from your server
Permissions
Local notifications
chunks.text:
## Local notifications

`local-notifications` installs `@capacitor/local-notifications` and declares `POST_NOTIFICATIONS`. Ask with `requestPermission("notifications")`, then schedule:

```ts
import { onLocalNotificationTapped, scheduleNotification } from "denext/mobile";

const id = await scheduleNotification({
  title: "Stand-up",
  body: "In 10 minutes",
  trigger: { type: "weekly", weekday: 2, hour: 9, minute: 50 }, // Mondays (1 = Sunday)
  data: { path: "/standup" }, // a tap opens /standup
  channelId: "reminders", // Android
  categoryId: "reminder", // its action buttons
});
onLocalNotificationTapped(({ actionId }) => console.log(actionId)); // "tap" or an action id
```

Triggers: `date`, `interval` (`seconds`, optionally `repeats`, at least 60 s when repeating), `daily`, `weekly`, `monthly`, `yearly`, and `calendar` (any date components; `repeats: false` for the next match only); none means now. Months are 1–12 and times are local. `cancelNotification(id | ids)`, `cancelAllNotifications()` and `pendingNotifications()` manage them; `createNotificationChannel` / `deleteNotificationChannel` / `listNotificationChannels` are Android's channels (a no-op elsewhere). A tap routes through the same rules as a push tap (`data.path`, or `data.url` under the deep-link acceptance rules), once per tap, cold start included; `useLocalNotificationTapped` is the hook form.

`setNotificationCategories([...])` registers the action buttons (text-input actions included) a notification shows with `categoryId`. The call replaces every earlier category, so pass the full set. **On iOS the categories also apply to remote pushes**: they live in the app's one `UNUserNotificationCenter`, so a push whose `aps.category` names one shows its buttons, and the tapped button reaches `onPushTapped` as `actionId`. On Android they apply to local notifications only (FCM draws its own notification). On the web a notification without a trigger shows through the Notifications API; anything later rejects (no scheduler). Android 12+ may deliver an exact time a few minutes late unless the user allows exact alarms, and Google Play allows the plugin's `SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM` only for alarm and calendar apps.

chunks.title: Biometrics
Clerk in the shell
chunks.text:
## Clerk in the shell

`denext/mobile/clerk` lets the app's own Clerk provider — `<ClerkProvider>` from `@clerk/nextjs` or `@clerk/react`, the one the web build uses — sign in inside the iOS and Android app, as `denext/desktop/clerk` does in a Deno Desktop window. Set it up once:

```sh
denext mobile add clerk --scheme myapp   # auth session + secure storage + the scheme
```

```ts
// instrumentation-client.ts (an App Router app; the top of the entry in a SPA)
import { installClerkMobileBridge } from "denext/mobile/clerk";
installClerkMobileBridge({ scheme: "myapp", nativeClerk: true });
```

- `nativeClerk` switches the clerk-js instance the provider loads into native mode, as `@clerk/electron/react` does with its bundled one: no cookies (a WebView's cookies for Clerk's domain are third-party), the client JWT in the Keychain / Keystore (`secureStore`), sent as `Authorization`; the session survives a relaunch. Without the secure-storage plugin the token stays in memory, never in the WebView's IndexedDB.
- Google / GitHub open in `openAuthSession` (`ASWebAuthenticationSession` on iOS, a Custom Tab on Android) and come back to `myapp://app/`. Only this session's redirect (scheme, host and path) is accepted, one flow at a time, and a Clerk callback outside a session never reaches `onDeepLink`. On Android the callback travels through the app's intent filter, so another app registered for the same scheme could receive it; see [Limitations](/docs/limitations).
- Passkeys: a page at `capacitor://localhost` / `https://localhost` cannot use WebAuthn for Clerk's relying party, so a passkey sign-in continues in the auth session on Clerk's hosted page (its own domain), with `state` and S256 PKCE bound to the page (`startClerkMobileBrowserSignIn`). Create passkeys on the web. `passkeys: "none"` hides them.
- Clerk side: add `myapp://app/` to Native applications → Allowlist for mobile SSO redirect, and `capacitor://localhost` and `https://localhost` to the instance's `allowed_origins` (Backend API `PATCH /v1/instance`): native mode sends `Authorization` and the WebView adds `Origin`, which the Frontend API refuses together from an origin it does not allow. The shell's API calls go to your server with a bearer session token: list those origins in its `cors` too. [examples/clerk](/docs/examples/clerk) has the whole setup.

chunks.text:
### Channels and staged rollouts

One `createOtaHandler` can serve several release tracks. Each release is a normal export with its own `_denext/ota.json` (signed as usual); a channels file says which release each channel serves, and a staged rollout sends a candidate to a percentage of installs.

```bash
denext ota channel production releases/2026-09-20   # creates ota-channels.json
denext ota channel beta releases/2026-09-27
denext ota promote --channel beta --to production --percent 20   # staged rollout
denext ota promote --channel beta --to production --percent 50   # widen it
denext ota promote --channel beta --to production                # 100%: the new stable release
denext ota promote --to production --halt                        # stop a bad rollout
```

```ts
// the server
const ota = createOtaHandler({ channels: "ota-channels.json", basePath: "/mobile-ui", cors: true });

// the app
await checkForUiUpdate({
  baseUrl: "https://api.example.com/mobile-ui",
  channel: "beta",
  onNativeUpdateRequired: () => promptStoreUpdate({ appStoreId: "123456789" }),
});
```

- The app sends `x-denext-ota-channel` (absent: the file’s `default`) and `x-denext-ota-install-id` (`otaInstallId()`, a random id kept in `localStorage`) with the manifest request and every file download, so one check is served from one release. An unknown channel is not served, never swapped for another.
- A candidate goes to the installs whose bucket (SHA-256 of the channel, the candidate’s version and the install id) falls under `percent`. Each candidate picks a fresh cohort, raising the percent only adds devices, and no install id means the stable release. Manifests pass through untouched, so signatures verify exactly as before.
- `promote` refuses what devices would refuse anyway: an unsigned release onto a channel serving signed ones (`signature`), or a lower `sequence` than the channel’s devices may run (`downgrade`); `--force` overrides both. Halting a rollout does not downgrade devices that took the candidate: fix forward with a higher sequence. The channels file is re-read when it changes, so a promote needs no restart.

chunks.title: Native fingerprint
chunks.text:
## Native fingerprint

Whether a change can ship over the air depends on whether it touched the native layer. `denext mobile fingerprint` answers that with one hash (the Expo equivalent is `@expo/fingerprint`): the same value means the installed binaries can run the new UI; a different one means a new app build.

```bash
denext mobile fingerprint                         # the SHA-256, one line
denext mobile fingerprint --json > native.json    # { fingerprint, inputs: [...] }
denext mobile fingerprint --diff native.json      # which inputs changed since, and the verdict
denext mobile fingerprint --write                 # embed it in the native projects
```

It reads the Capacitor project at `--dir` (default: the current directory) and hashes:

- every file under `ios/` and `android/`, except build output and caches (`build/`, `DerivedData`, `Pods`, `.gradle`, `.cxx`, SwiftPM's `.build`), per-user and machine-local files (`xcuserdata`, `*.xcuserstate`, `local.properties`, `.idea`, `*.iml`, `.DS_Store`), signing material and build products (`*.jks`, `*.keystore`, `*.p12`, `*.mobileprovision`, `*.apk`, `*.aab`, `*.ipa`), and what `cap sync` copies in (the web UI in `App/public` and `assets/public`, the copied `capacitor.config.json`, `capacitor.plugins.json`, `config.xml`, and the generated Cordova plugin projects). Text files (no NUL byte in their first 8000 bytes) are hashed with CRLF turned into LF, so git's `autocrlf` on Windows does not change the result;
- `capacitor.config.*` without its `server` block, which `denext mobile dev` edits (a JSON config is compared by content, whatever its formatting);
- the installed version of `@capacitor/core`, `ios`, `android`, `cli`, and of every dependency or dev dependency in `package.json` that is a Capacitor plugin (a `@capacitor/` package, a `capacitor` field in its `package.json`, or a Cordova `plugin.xml`), resolved in `node_modules` from the project upwards as Node does. Other dependencies never count. Install packages first: a missing one prints a warning (and a missing `@capacitor/` package counts as `not installed`).

The fingerprint is lowercase hex SHA-256 over the line `denext-native-fingerprint-v1` followed by one `<key><TAB><sha256>` line per input, sorted by key as the OTA version is: a file's key is its project-relative path, a package's is `npm:<name>` with the SHA-256 of its version. The same checkout gives the same value on any machine and in any directory.

**The gate.** `--write` stores the fingerprint as the Info.plist string `DenextNativeFingerprint` and the AndroidManifest `<meta-data android:name="dev.denext.native.FINGERPRINT" android:value="…" />`, replacing an earlier value. Those two entries are left out of the hash, so writing them never changes it and a second run changes nothing. Stamp the matching manifest with `--native-fingerprint`, either the value itself or `auto` (computed for `--dir`):

```bash
denext mobile fingerprint --write          # before building the binary
denext ota manifest out --sign ota.key --native-fingerprint auto --dir .
```

A binary whose embedded fingerprint differs from the manifest's refuses the UI before downloading (code `native_mismatch`, returned by `checkForUiUpdate` and `prepareUiUpdate`). When either side has no fingerprint, the check is skipped, so apps and manifests from before it keep working. In a signed manifest the fingerprint is part of the signed payload (v3), so it cannot be stripped or swapped.

> **Warning:** **Binaries built before the gate.** An app binary whose OTA plugin predates the gate (template generation 3 or older, as written by denext 2.10.0-rc.2 and earlier) does not know the v3 payload: with a key embedded, it refuses a signed manifest that carries a fingerprint as `signature` (not `native_mismatch`), and it ignores the fingerprint of an unsigned one. Refusing is right (re-running `add-ota` to get the gate changes the native sources, so such a binary is on another native layer anyway); only the code differs. A version or build number committed to the native sources counts as a native change: set them on the build command line instead (see [Building in CI](#building-in-ci)).

chunks.title: iOS privacy manifest
chunks.text:
## iOS privacy manifest

Since May 1, 2024, App Store Connect refuses an app that calls one of Apple's [required-reason APIs](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/bundleresources/describing-use-of-required-reason-api) without declaring an approved reason in its `PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy`. None of the plugins `denext mobile add` pins ships a manifest of its own, so their use goes in the app's (as Capacitor's [privacy manifest guide](https://capacitorjs.com/docs/ios/privacy-manifest) says). Each capability declares what its iOS code calls, read from the pinned plugin's sources and denext's own templates, and `mobile add` merges it into `ios/App/App/PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy` (creating it, and adding it to the App target's Copy Bundle Resources). The merge only adds: your own categories, reasons, collected-data rows, `NSPrivacyTracking` and tracking domains stay as they are.

- `filesystem`: FileTimestamp `C617.1` (`stat()` returns the times of files in the app container).
- `document-picker`: FileTimestamp `3B52.1` (the picked file's modification date).
- `social-login`: UserDefaults `CA92.1` (the plugin keeps provider state there). `background`: UserDefaults `CA92.1` (the runner's key-value store). `add-ota` (not a capability, same merge): UserDefaults `CA92.1`.
- `widget`: UserDefaults `1C8F.1` (App Group) in the app and in the `DenextWidgets` extension's own manifest. `share-extension`: FileTimestamp `C617.1` in the app and in `DenextShareExtension` (old shared files are pruned by date).
- `sentry`: no API (sentry-cocoa ships its own manifest), but the collected data: crash, performance and other diagnostic data, not linked, not tracking, App Functionality.
- `@capacitor/preferences` (which `restore` uses when you add it): UserDefaults `CA92.1`, merged by `mobile privacy --write`. `tracking` needs no reason, but an app that asks for tracking permission tracks: the check warns until `NSPrivacyTracking` is true, with your tracking domains listed.
- Every other capability was checked and uses none. None of them reads disk space or boot time; if your own native code does, add `E174.1` / `35F9.1` yourself (the merge keeps them).

```bash
denext mobile privacy            # print the manifest and what is wrong with it
denext mobile privacy --write    # merge the entries of every installed capability (never removes)
denext mobile privacy --check    # exit 1 on an error: a CI gate
```

The check validates each category and reason against Apple's list (and refuses the SDK-only `0A2A.1` / `C56D.1` in an app), the collected-data types and purposes, tracking without tracking domains, the entries the installed capabilities need, and whether Xcode copies the file into the app. `denext doctor` reports the same as an advisory line when the project is a Capacitor project. The App Store "nutrition label" (what your server collects about users) is yours to fill in App Store Connect; the manifest covers what the app itself does.

chunks.title: App Store review
chunks.text:
## App Store review

Apple's guideline [4.2 (Minimum Functionality)](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/#minimum-functionality) rejects an app that is "a repackaged website", and a WebView shell is where reviewers look for one; a Capacitor app with location and sharing [was still rejected](https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/812889) as not robust enough. What reviewers can see decides it:

- **It is an app, not a site.** The UI ships in the binary (the export, `webDir: "out"`), never a `server.url` pointing at your website. Native navigation (a tab bar, stack transitions, the back gesture), system bars and safe areas, haptics and the keyboard behave like the platform's.
- **Native capabilities that matter to the app's job**, visible in the review build: push, widgets, Live Activities, a share extension, quick actions, biometric unlock, the camera or document picker, deep links. Name them in the review notes.
- **Offline behaviour.** The app opens without a network and says what is going on: cached data where it has some, otherwise a proper screen, never a blank page or a browser error. `denext mobile add offline-screen` writes `public/offline.html` and points Capacitor's `server.errorPath` at it (shown when the content cannot load), and `installOfflineScreen()` from `denext/mobile` covers the page while the device is offline.
- **No flow that only works in an external browser.** Sign-in uses `openAuthSession` (a system sheet that returns to the app) or the native Apple / Google sheets; links to other sites open in the in-app browser (`openExternal`), not by leaving the app.
- **Sign-in requirements.** An app that offers Google (or another third-party) sign-in also offers Sign in with Apple (guideline 4.8; `signInWithApple()`). The review notes carry a demo account.
- **Account deletion.** An app that creates accounts lets users delete them in the app (5.1.1(v)): `session.deleteAccount()` from `nativeSession`, or `POST /auth/account/delete` (denextAuth serves it when the adapter has `deleteUser`).
- **Privacy.** A valid privacy manifest, a usage string for every permission the plugins ask for, and purchases of digital goods through in-app purchase (3.1.1).

chunks.title: Guideline 4.2 checklist
Crash reporting
chunks.text:
## Crash reporting

`denext mobile add sentry` installs `@sentry/capacitor` 4.4.0 with its sibling web SDK `@sentry/browser` 10.69.0 (the exact version it depends on; keep the two in step). Native crashes are reported by sentry-cocoa and sentry-android, JavaScript errors by the web SDK. It supports Capacitor 8; on iOS it installs through Swift Package Manager only (a CocoaPods project moves to SPM first).

```ts
import { initCrashReporting } from "denext/mobile";

await initCrashReporting({
  dsn: "https://<key>@o0.ingest.sentry.io/<project>",
  sdk: () => import("@sentry/capacitor"),
  sibling: () => import("@sentry/browser"), // or @sentry/react
  environment: "production",
  options: { tracesSampleRate: 0.1 },
});
```

The SDKs load only when this runs. The release is the UI version the page was served with, the `version` of its `_denext/ota.json` (`spa.ota: true`), so every over-the-air UI reports under its own release and its stack traces match its own source maps. No `dist` is set by default: one UI version runs on several binaries, and Sentry matches uploaded files only when the dist is equal.

**Hidden source maps.** `denext export --sourcemaps hidden` (or `DENEXT_SOURCEMAPS=hidden`) builds external source maps, then moves them out of the export into `.denext/sourcemaps/` next to a copy of the JavaScript they map, at the same paths. Nothing in `out/` references or contains a map, and the OTA manifest never lists one. Upload them under the same release:

```bash
denext export --sourcemaps hidden
npx @sentry/cli sourcemaps upload \
  --org "$SENTRY_ORG" --project "$SENTRY_PROJECT" \
```
